name: Secure Coding Checklist
description: This module is a pre-completion checklist for secure coding work: a short set of checks to run before calling a secure coding task done.
content:
This module is a pre-completion checklist for secure coding work: a short set of checks to run before calling a secure coding task done.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. When secure coding decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
2. Prefer explicit, readable secure coding solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
3. Surface known limitations of a chosen secure coding approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
4. Re-check edge cases relevant to secure coding (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
5. Document any non-obvious secure coding decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
6. Check that secure coding terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
7. Keep secure coding outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
8. When multiple secure coding strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
9. Before starting secure coding work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
10. State assumptions about secure coding explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
11. Prefer the simplest secure coding approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
12. Validate secure coding outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not silently drop secure coding edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Do not skip documenting secure coding assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Avoid introducing new secure coding abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Avoid mixing unrelated secure coding concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of secure coding correctness.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for secure coding, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
